body:
These surrogate activities are usually less satisfying than the
pursuit of real goals: i.e., the physical necessities of life. The
proof of this, Unabomer maintains, is the driving force to constantly
do something new or better which is found in most modern technological
societies. He writes that people who accumulate tremendous amounts of
wealth (far more then they need), or the scientist who is constantly
looking for new scientific mysteries to solve, are perfect examples of
this drive to always want more, new, or better material possessions.
Because of two aspects of our modern technological society, Unabomer
writes, people claim that they are not interested in pursuing the
goals of nourishment and shelter. The first aspect is the ease with
which people can fulfill these needs. The second aspect is the need
for them to give up their autonomy in order to have those needs
fulfilled. In short, in order to have their food, drink, and shelter
easily available, they must work within the society, and must place
restrictions on their own actions [FC 1995, para. 41].

Unabomer thinks that the fourth part of his power process, gaining
autonomy, is vitally important. It is, he argues, necessary for most
people to have some form of autonomy in working toward their goals.
They need it in order to fulfill their power process. By power
process, he means the goals, effort, attainment, and autonomy
mentioned at the beginning of this chapter. People, he argues, need to
express some of their own initiative and direction, and have some
control toward working to completion of their goals. If they are in a
rigidly controlled organization which predetermines everything they
must do toward completion of their goal, they will not have their
power process fulfilled [FC 1995, para. 42]. Unabomer qualifies this
statement by saying that not all people need the same sort of autonomy
in order to gain the power process. He thinks that there are people
who have only a weak need for the power process, and who can find
fulfillment of the power process by completing tasks under the
direction of their superiors [FC 1995, para. 43].

In conclusion, Unabomer thinks that most people need autonomy, by
which he seems to mean an almost complete independence from society,
in order to gain the self-esteem that is necessary for them to remain
healthy human beings. He also seems to argue that, hand in hand with
needing autonomy, any activity beyond providing the necessities of
life is superfluous. If people do not have this autonomy, he argues,
they run the danger of becoming demoralized or bored, and therefore by
inference, suffer from the same symptoms the aristocrats of the past
experienced: e.g., boredom, decay of their moral standard, and
hedonism.



Industrial-Technical Society

The problems plaguing technological society, Unabomer asserts, come
from the fact that modern society requires most of its members to live
in an environment radically different from that in which man evolved.
While he acknowledges that ``not all was sweetness and light'' [FC
1995, para. 45] in pre-industrial societies, he thinks that there was
much less in the way of mental malaise. He gives several examples of
problems that cause difficulties:

  ...excessive density of population, isolation of man from nature,
  excessive rapidity of social change, and the break-down of natural
  and small-scale communities such as the extended family, the
  village, or the tribe [FC 1995, para. 47].

Each of these problems, Unabomer indicates, can be traced at least
partially back to the advent of the Industrial Revolution, and the
rapid growth of technology that it entailed. This severely disrupted
the ``natural'' framework of the social structure people were used to.
Unabomer claims that this lack of a stable framework caused the decay
of traditional values. This breakdown also implies the breakdown of
the small-scale social groups mentioned above; the extended family was
disrupted as were the small town communities.

The breakdown came from several different directions. One of the most
prominent came from the fact that modern society often requires people
to move from location to location for their work. The second reason,
Unabomer writes, is that modern society must weaken the ties between
family members in order to function efficiently. Overall, this section
is confusing. The Unabomer tries to support his assertions by giving
examples of problems. He writes about the stigma that American society
attaches to nepotism, as compared to both older American and English
societies, and to other cultures. He points out how some countries,
for example South America, have inefficient industrial-technological
production and innovation. He concludes that in order for an
industrial-technological society to properly function, it can only
support ``small-scale communities that are emasculated, tamed and made
into tools of the system'' [FC 1995, para. 52].

While Unabomer thinks that the extensive changes in the social
framework, such as the breakdown of the communities and the
overcrowding mentioned above, are one source of psychological problems
in society, he does not think they are the main source. Unabomer
claims that some pre-industrial cities were very crowded, but the
inhabitants there did not exhibit the same degree of psychological
maladjustment that people in modern cities do. Unabomer also claims
that the frontier settlers in America lived in relative isolation, and
displayed none of the problems above.

The difference between pre-industrial society and contemporary ones,
the Unabomer writes, is that modern man has change imposed upon him,
as opposed to the time when the country was so wide open that man was
able to live in relative isolation, and therefore live with relative
autonomy. In conclusion, Unabomer thinks that the crowded,
over-populated cities that exist now disrupt our autonomy and
therefore disrupt the power process. Without this power process, we
are not freely acting individuals. Without this power process, the
society cannot fail to degenerate.


On Freedom

Technology, Unabomer writes, is incompatible with the nature of human
freedom as he sees it. Freedom, as Unabomer writes, is the ability to
go about setting goals and then struggling to complete those goals.
These goals cannot be the ``artificial'' goals he attacks earlier;
they cannot, for example, be scientific pursuit, sports or hobbies.
Unabomer thinks that the only good goals are those which help man
determine his own own life-and-death existence. This means shelter
from the elements, clothing, gathering food, and defense against any
other threats.

He writes that ``one gets the impression'' that older societies - the
Indian Nations of the New England region, or the cities of Italy
during the Renaissance for example - allowed much more autonomy than
their contemporary counterparts. Unabomer argues that people had more
autonomy because there were ``no well-organized police, no rapid
communications, no surveillance cameras, and no dossiers of personal
information held by the authorities'' [FC 1995, para. 95].

Unabomer points out that, in modern society, freedom in the political
sphere is severely limited by the controlling class; e.g., the wealthy
citizens, or powerful government officials. He argues that the freedom
of the press is a case in point. While, he argues, the freedom of the
press is certainly useful as a means to limit the accumulation of
political power by any one group, it is not as useful as we might
think. It is, he argues, of little use to the average citizen. The
problem is that the media are such large producers of information,
that the lone voice cannot be heard against the glut of information
being put out every day. Unabomer writes that anybody with even a
little money can have his writing printed, or sent out onto the
Internet; but it will have no practical effect because it will not be
in the public eye for long, if at all.

The problem with freedom in the political sphere is not only the
problem of not being heard. It extends, Unabomer writes, to the very
conception and acceptance of what freedom means. Freedom, he argues,
is something most of us only believe we have. Moreover, he argues that
few people really know what freedom is at all. This belief in freedom,
Unabomer warns, is a falsehood perpetuated by the upper class. Freedom
in the United States to pursue economic goals, Unabomer writes, is
present only because the economic upper class want a growing economy
in order to gain more wealth. The freedom of people in socialist
countries, he argues, is only the freedom to work for the interests of
the state. What kind of freedom, Unabomer asks us, is living our lives
according to the mandate of others?


Historical Principles

Unabomer asserts several historical principles as a foundation for his
later argument:

  Small changes in society will not affect the long-term historical
  trend.

  Large changes that affect the long-term historical trend will affect
  more than one area of society.

  Changes that do have a long-term effect will have unforeseen
  consequences.

  Because of these previous principles, it is clear that a new society
  cannot be designed on paper.

Unabomer argues that the American Revolution was an example of these
principles. Unabomer claims that America would have had representative
democracy regardless of whether or not the revolution occurred.
Unabomer believes that the American Revolution was not necessary in
order for the country to become a representative democracy. As a sort
of convoluted proof, Unabomer points out that many other
English-speaking countries have evolved into representative
democracies without a revolution. Therefore, he argues, America would
have also become a representative democracy regardless of whether or
not the American Revolution occurred.

Unabomer concludes that people need to use common sense when applying
these rules, but he thinks that the principles should be in everyone's
mind when analyzing a societal problem. If a person draws conclusions
that conflict with these principles, he writes, they should reexamine
the problem and ``retain the conclusion only if one has good, solid
reasons for doing so'' [FC 1995, para. 110].



Against Industrial Society

The next five sections of Unabomer's manifesto (starting at paragraph
99) explain why Unabomer thinks that an industrial society is
incompatible with his ideal society. His main points are:

  History has shown industrialization to strengthen the system at the
  cost of personal autonomy.

  The whole system of laissez-faire economics not only dictates many
  of our actions, but also constitutes an unnatural alteration of
  human behavior.

  The technical and social interdependencies of technological society
  force these unnatural alterations on any community.

  Technology impacts everyone, and forces physical changes on the
  environment.

  These changes cannot be personally controlled, or even moderated.

  The simpler problems in our society prove to be difficult to solve;
  how can we expect to be able to solve problems caused by technology?

Unabomer concludes that it is impossible to resolve his concerns about
freedom with technology. He raises concerns that technology will
evolve to the point that all natural freedom will be lost. With
government - or corporate - sponsored mental conditioning and genetic
re-engineering possibilities on the future horizon, Unabomer wants the
development of high technology stopped, and wants all instances of
high technology destroyed.

Before I proceed, I should explain what is meant by high technology.
In Unabomer's work, and in many other writings, a distinction is made
between types of technology. Sometimes they are called big and small
technology, sometimes they are called high and low technology. Big
technology is any technology that is complicated, and requires a large
number of workers and materials to make. It has complex
interdependencies that must be in place in order for it to function.
Small technology is sometimes thought of as primitive technology. It
is not so complex as to require many men or materials. It does not
depend on a variety of outside elements. An example that Unabomer
gives is the difference between a refrigerator and an ice-box. The
former requires a great deal of labor, many complex parts, many
different physical materials, and is dependent on outside elements
like electricity. An ice-box, on the other hand, is fairly simple in
design, and simply requires ice to operate in the expected manner.


Revolution Against Technology

What is the route to Unabomer's goal of no high technology? Unabomer's
ideology is to fight technology by creating a new world-view, where
society rejects the complicated, interdependent, technology currently
being developed. The vast amount of money and work required to
maintain high technology requires man to conform to a set of rules,
usually at the cost of personal autonomy. The Unabomer considers this
forced conformity to be evil. He writes that nature holds a perfect
counter-ideal to technology. A world of small technology, and of small
social groups would solve the problems of autonomy and loss of
individuality which Unabomer thinks high technology causes.

In order to gain popular support for his ideology, Unabomer tells us
that his strategy must take place on two levels. One level addresses
itself to the intellectuals. It is one that uses logic and reason to
convince intelligent people that his revolution is necessary and would
be advantageous. The second level is aimed at what he calls the
unthinking masses. This second level sounds like a propaganda blitz,
though Unabomer is very clear that he does not mean it to take the
form of short-term and irrational, ultimately useless, catch-phrases.
However, it must present the conflict between nature and technology in
simple and ``unambiguous terms.''

Unabomer thinks that a conflict between the technological elite and
the masses will be the main cause for the revolution. On the one hand,
the technological elite will fight to maintain their position. On the
other other hand, the masses will struggle to destroy that technology.
That conflict, the Unabomer warns, must not be expanded to encompass
other problems, since technology is at the root of many of those other
problems. Unabomer stresses that this is not a political conflict, and
that revolutionaries should avoid trying to assume political power
until after the majority of the population are won over to his
ideology. Unabomer also argues that the revolution cannot take place
in just one country. This revolution, he argues, needs to be global in
order to totally succeed. For, writes Unabomer, if the global
revolution does not succeed, countries that maintain technology may
exert control over countries that have rejected technology. This may
not necessarily be a bad outcome. Dictatorships, he argues, have a
tendency to dissolve more quickly than democracies. Unabomer is
obviously implying that the revolution may take more then one stage in
order to succeed, and that the revolutionaries will keep trying if
they fail the first time.


Kindred Spirits?

The Unabomer's manuscript often rambles on seemingly irrelevant
tangents, and his tirade against leftists is, at best, only marginally
related to his thesis. However, there is a core set of positions that
can be extracted from the document. The three main positions revolve
around the same concerns that some environmentalists, Luddites, and
other anti-technology groups have been arguing about for many years.
The three main positions are:

  Technology is responsible for most of the problems in modern
  technological society.

  Nature without high-technology is the perfect environment for us.

  An anti-technology revolution is the only way to get rid of
  high-technology.

I was interested in finding out whether or not there were more
developed versions of the Unabomer's thesis. Had other authors written
extensive works that show the roots of the Unabomer's ideas? I had
certainly expected to find kindred spirits to the Unabomer's
anti-technology philosophy, but I was still surprised at the enormous
collection of materials available. I think it is important to examine
the Unabomer's thesis in terms of other, more powerful,
anti-technology works.




  An End in Itself?
  Environmental Disregard
  Autonomy in a Technological Society
  Anti-technology Revolution?

An End in Itself?

In Technology-Humanism or Nihilism, Gregory H. Davis writes that,
since before the use of fire, mankind has used technology to control
nature. Mankind has used technology to shape nature toward meeting
their needs. But modern technology is fundamentally different from the
older technology, argue philosophers like Jacques Ellul. This modern
technology operates on a global, even on an inter-planetary scale. It
creates substances indestructible by nature, and spreads out to affect
the entire globe. It is no longer localized and temporary; it is
global and permanent [Davis 1981, p. 1].

Human error and human emotions become a very significant problem when
powerful technology becomes available to us. Weapons of mass
destruction, such as the nuclear bomb, are capable of destroying the
world. Technologies such as pesticides are capable of causing
widespread damage to the environment. Chemical technologies are
capable of causing widespread death and illness to any living thing
that they touch. The problem is that technology is viewed as being
important in terms of making profit. No firm will take twenty years to
study the long term effects of a new pesticide. It simply is not
profitable enough. Also of concern is the realm of the artificial
becoming accepted as the natural world. Some examples are gender
switching operations, artificial prolongation of life through devices
like electronic heart pace-makers, chemical substances to regulate our
body functions, and substitution of television and other mass
entertainment for the real-life experience of simply going out and
meeting with other people [Davis 1981, p. 2-6].

In order to understand our lives, we must study the impact of
technology on our social framework. People like Ellul, Davis writes,
argue that our technology is a technology without limits. It is a
technology that invades all aspects of our lives, and affects
everyone. The disturbing aspect of this is that it orients people
toward more advanced technology. People begin, Davis argues, to look
toward technological advancement as an end in and of itself, rather
than as a means toward a more concrete, attainable, and good goal:
e.g., really stop world hunger, or really help the environment. In
other words, we pursue technology for its own sake, always trying to
build bigger and better technology as fast as we can. We never really
try and fully use the technology we have already developed [Davis
1981, p. 7].

This attitude, writes Davis, relegates other standards, such as
humanistic or ecological standards, into the background of society.
Factors that contribute to the happiness or well-being of the people
or society is ignored. Concerns about ``happiness, aesthetics,
environmental quality, uniqueness and originality'' [Davis 1981, p. 4]
are not important to the society.

While the individual who is proud of human achievements may begin to
have misgivings about technology, the system works against him. Any
criticism of technology is crushed by the society that sees technology
as an end in and of itself. For example, Davis writes that, in 1976,
three management level engineers at General Electric resigned to
publicly protest the poor safety guidelines for nuclear power plants.
Likewise, two scientists at Livermore Radiation Laboratory disclosed
that the minimum radiation exposure safety levels set by the
government were dangerously high. In response, one of the scientists
had his research staff removed by the government [Davis 1981, p. 14].

Why does this phenomenon of technology becoming more important than
safety or happiness occur? According to Davis, it seems to develop out
of the desire to control nature. Davis writes about what he calls the
control ethic. Since technology allows man to rise above nature, it
allows humans to feel free of natural constraints. These constraints
include movement from one location to another, food supply, and
shelter. Similarly, Richard B. Norgaard argues that technology has
made people think they have a greater amount of freedom than their
forefathers did. An easy-to-tap energy source, fossil fuels, and the
rise of technological aid has given us the ability to have a great
deal of immediate control over nature (as opposed to being able to
predict and control the long term effects of our actions). We can use
the farmer as an example. With the tractor and chemicals, with easy
transportation and storage, the farmer can till his soil with ease,
plant without worrying about crop rotation, harvest his crops quickly,
and transport them across the country. This control over the land, can
give people a greater sense of freedom; they appear to no longer be at
the mercy of nature [Norgaard 1994, p. 43-45]. However, it is clear
that technology cannot solve all our problems. The United States grows
an overabundance of food every year. Grain silos are filled with food
that is exported or sits and rots in disuse [Lunger 1991]. We even pay
farmers not to grow crops [Runge 1995], and proposals are made to
export our surplus food supply to needy countries [Atwood 1995].
Paradoxically we have tens of millions of people in the United States
going hungry every year [Express 1996].

Technology gives us the resources to shelter, clothe, and feed
everyone, but does not give us the social structure to do so. This is
a social failing, but we do not pay attention to that; we still pour
research funds into biotechnology in an attempt to grow food faster,
and more efficiently [Biotechnology Industry Organization 1989]. Why
is it that development of technology to distribute food to the hungry
is not considered more important than producing even more food we will
probably not distribute?


Environmental Disregard

Besides the problem of misdirected efforts concerning why we want
technological advancement, discussed in section 4.1, there is also a
great deal of concern about the danger that technology poses to the
environment. The Unabomer only briefly touches on these subjects,
writing about the need to conserve resources [FC 1995, para. 138],
promoting what is usually known as primitive appropriate technology
[FC 1995, paragraphs 208-212], and writing about whether or not
reverence toward nature can be used to further the anti-technology
revolution [FC 1995, endnote 26]. However, I think that the Unabomer's
argument could be fortified by drawing upon the work of the
environmentalist and conservationist movements. From within these
movements, authors have produced a great deal of work that can inspire
people to reexamine man's use of technology. The arguments against
pollution and against the depletion of our natural resources, for
example, are very powerful.

Davis writes extensively about the dangers to the world caused by
chemicals, nuclear waste, and other pollutants. The problem is that
mankind, with the modern technology available to him, can now inflict
permanent damage onto the environment. Davis gives us examples of
pollution of the atmosphere, sea, fresh water, food sources, and
workplace. This pollution leads to the problems of obtaining clean
air, usable food and water, and to the problem of trying not to get
cancer or other diseases from living in a modern technological
society. It is not just that people are not concerned with the
problems these chemicals can cause; it is that most of the time people
do not realize the dangers until it is simply too late. Davis writes
about the long-term problems associated with certain pesticides, power
sources, drugs, and other technologies [Davis 1981, p. 55-59] which
were thought at the time to be beneficial and harmless. In fact, it
turned out that some of them were poisons. The pesticide DBCP caused
``skin irritation, continual nose bleeding, respiratory difficulties,
and sterility.'' [Davis 1981, p. 206] The pesticide Kepone caused
``loss of memory, liver malfunction, dizziness, weight loss,
sterility, aching and brittle joints, nervous disorders and
irritability, defective eyesight and trembling'' [Davis 1981, p. 206].
After the effects were discovered, these chemicals were banned from
further use. However, the problem is not always solvable by simply
pointing out the damage that can be done to the land, and to people.
In some cases, the technologically-oriented people in contemporary
society simply do not care about the damage they cause.

Authors like Aldo Leopold, Wendell Berry, Leo Marx, and many others
have written about the beauty of nature, and about callous disregard
for nature that technological man exhibits. These authors show us that
in late 20th century cultures many people have an almost wanton
disregard for the land and for animals, and that they only view land
as a resource to be exploited for profit.

Aldo Leopold's extremely popular and very moving book, titled A Sand
County Almanac [Leopold 1989], gives an excellent example of this
problem, and also gives the reader a different perspective on the
``use'' of land. Leopold's book points out the beauty and power of
nature from a personal perspective. His essays are a corner-stone of
the environmentalist movement, and they force the reader to examine
his own appreciation of the beauty in nature, and force him to examine
the damage man has inflicted on nature. Leopold allows the reader a
brief and poignant glimpse into the natural world surrounding his farm
in Wisconsin. In each chapter, one for each month, he writes about the
animals his fancy was particularly struck by, and he usually writes a
little bit about how the local ecology, and how that animal's species,
were probably both damaged in years past by a disregard for the
sanctity of nature. The chapters make the reader think both about the
harmony that nature is usually in (see the next paragraph for an
example of what this harmony is), and about the inevitable damage
caused by man's attempts to impose his control over the land.

The second section of Leopold's book encompasses a more detailed
example of the damage man has done to nature. The harmony of nature,
Leopold points out, is that all the elements interact with one another
to form the ecosystem. A specific example is how the swampy nature of
the wetlands in northern Wisconsin helped maintain the existence of
the surrounding prairie lands. Men tried to farm this marshland, and
drained the water in order to expose farmable land. Huge swathes of
peat were exposed to the sun in the process. Later, the farmers found
that the land was prone to heavy frosts, and so they abandoned their
attempts at farming the lands. Neglected, the peat moss beds grew dry.
During a hot summer, they would catch fire, and that fire would
spread, destroying much of the surrounding meadow lands. As a result
of the fires, wooded fields would spring up in the former meadows, and
so the meadows and marshlands began to die away, replaced by farms and
forests. Obviously the ecological damage had been tremendous, but the
men who drained the marshes had no awareness of, or simply did not
care for, the delicate balance of nature which the local wildlife
depended on to survive. Leopold points out that, while
conservationists repaired some of the damage done, the entire repair
project can be called into question because of other damage being
inflicted on the land. Why, he asks, does the government build a road
right through the lands they are nominally trying to save? The reason,
Leopold writes, is that people do not appreciate the wilderness for
its own sake. Generally, people believe that they should be able to
tour the wilderness from the comfort of their cars, and not have to
leave their modern conveniences in order to appreciate nature. Of
course this is a self-defeating cycle, they fix the land, try and
restore it to a wilderness, and then plow a great wound into the
middle of it all, laying down their concrete and steel so that they
may enjoy the wild from inside their cars.

The third section of Leopold's book examines the almost spiritual
quality that wilderness can provide. He argues that the mechanization
of the land, the destruction of wilderness, is destroying something of
great value. It destroys our heritage, and dulls our appreciation of
the natural world. Leopold concludes by arguing that we must examine
the ethical and aesthetic values of our technology, not just the
economic ones. We must try and preserve the ''integrity, stability,
and beauty of the biotic community'' [Leopold 1989, p. 224-225].

The farmers who drained the marshlands were only interested in their
farming and, in their zeal to expand the farmable land, they managed
to seriously damage the surrounding nature. Davis, Leopold, and
Norgaard can actually all be tied in to one concept: Modern men use
technology without regard or deep examination of what their impact on
nature and society will be. Norgaard explains that the
Judeo-Christian-Islamic tradition tends to place man above the rest of
nature. The religious concepts tended to split nature into distinct
individual parts: God moved up the chain of nature, creating heaven,
earth, water, vegetation, the sun and the moon, sea and air creatures,
land creatures, and finally man [Wansbrough 1989, Genesis 1]. Man was
considered distinct from, and ruler of, the rest of nature.

This view, Norgaard argues, leads Western civilization to regard
nature both as something man is meant to control and dominate, and as
something that is made up of individual parts where the whole is not
harmed if one part is destroyed. Norgaard argues that the biologist
uses the analogy of a machine of lifeless parts when working in his
field, and many economists explain the accumulation of wealth without
examining people and how they interact outside of an economic model:
i.e., the non-rational actor, the illogical and emotional part of man
[Norgaard 1994, p. 182]. These views, Norgaard argues, have led modern
technological society to place the accumulation of scientific
knowledge and material wealth above the happiness of people in
society, or the welfare of the ecology.

Mankind has steadily depleted the planet's fuel sources, poured
enormous amounts of chemicals into the air, and has dramatically
increased the earth's population count. It has caused tremendous
damage to the environment [Norgaard 1994, p. 184]. I think that one of
the best summaries of this phenomenon comes from Lynn White, Jr.

  Despite Copernicus, all of the cosmos rotates around our little
  globe. Despite Darwin, we are not, in our hearts, part of the
  natural process. We are superior to nature, contemptuous of it,
  willing to use it for our slightest whim [White 1967, p. 51].

We are willing to use technology to bend nature to our will, and have
no qualms about causing widespread damage to the ecosystem. That
attitude will be our downfall if it continues. Viewing the skyline of
major cities like Los Angeles, California, and Chicago, Illinois,
where you can actually see the pollution hovering in thick clouds over
the city, you can form an idea of what could happen to the entire
world. If the environmental damage goes too far, we will not have any
alternative but to live in the completely technological society,
wearing air-filters when we move about outside. In case one is tempted
to dismiss this as something that might occur only in the far future,
one should realize that the low-level ozone, otherwise known as smog
[Wilson 1995], pollution in California is already so bad that state
health officials occasionally issue alerts which warn some people
against venturing outdoors [South Coast Air Quality Management
District 1996]. The pollution is so bad that Los Angeles health
officials post warnings that instruct people to not swim in the ocean
off the local beaches for at least three days after a storm [Guide
1996].

If we view nature as simply a collection of useful pieces of property
for our sole enjoyment and use, to use up and discard as we please, is
it also possible that we view our fellow man the same way? I believe
so, and this is why our discussion of nature is so important in the
context of the Unabomer. In the next section, we will start to examine
some of the problems that mankind has in the technological workplace.



Autonomy in a Technological Society

A major part of Unabomer's thesis revolves around the belief that
people lack autonomy, or control, of their lives. This lack of
control, the Unabomer argues, results in a multitude of sociological
problems. He lays out how he thinks the sociological problems are
interrelated, and gives us a diagram (See figure 4.1 for a
representation of his diagram.):

  Common-sense understanding of human nature tells one that lack of
  goals whose attainment requires effort leads to boredom and that
  boredom, long continued, often leads eventually to depression.
  Failure to obtain goals leads to frustration and lowering of
  self-esteem. Frustration leads to anger, anger to aggression, often
  in the form of spouse or child abuse. It has been shown that
  long-continued frustration commonly leads to depression and that
  depression tends to cause guilt, sleep disorders, eating disorders
  and bad feelings about oneself. Those who are tending toward
  depression seek pleasure as an antidote; hence insatiable hedonism
  and excessive sex, with perversions as a means of getting new kicks.
  Boredom too tends to cause excessive pleasure-seeking since, lacking
  other goals, people often use pleasure as a goal. See accompanying
  diagram [FC 1995, endnote 6].



Figure 4.1: Symptoms that arise from deprivation of the power process

One should not dismiss this as popular psychology (thoughts on
psychology that have no basis in reality). In her book I'm
Dysfunctional, You're Dysfunctional, Wendy Kaminer gives us some
insights about almost exactly the problems the Unabomer is concerned
about. Kaminer provides a witty, scathing, review of the psychological
problems some people are carrying around with them. These people, we
will refer to them as co-dependents, she writes, have started to call
themselves victims. They lament their problems to therapy groups; they
are depressed about their jobs or personal life, and they have become
addicted to the self-help market. They go onto national television
talk-shows and publicly proclaim that they are sick, and need help.
These are not people with severe mental problems. They are not
considered to be social deviants. In fact, the problems these
co-dependents complain about, as Kaminer points out, are considered
fairly normal in our society. Kaminer writes that this society is
inclined to tell a person that he or she is ``in denial'' if he or she
claims to be happy. Kaminer examines this problem by studying the
theme of co-dependency that is so popular today. She examines the
popular belief that people must depend on others in order to live
fulfilled lives. She questions why co-dependents seem to ``want help''
by looking at the rise of support groups, recovery seminars, new age
spirituality, and self-help groups. The problem is not just that
people in this modern society have difficult lives, it is that they do
not believe the problems can be solved without outside help. Kaminer
argues that these co-dependents are losing, or have already lost,
their individuality, are having their identity consumed by their
community. She argues that co-dependents need to start looking at some
of their unhappiness as normal, and that people need to be willing to
take control of their lives without a support group to guide them
every step of the way. Kaminer concludes that ``losing faith in your
own willfulness and capacity to act, you eventually lose freedom''
[Kaminer 1992, p.  151].

What will happen in a society that extols the ``virtues'' of
submitting your will and identity to others, supposedly for your own
good? On the face of it, this may not seem to be related to the
Unabomer's thesis. I argue that, in fact, it provides vital support to
his argument. The lack of autonomy that the Unabomer asserts in his
manuscript can be linked to the sense of helplessness that Kaminer
discusses.

Davis asserts, and shows some statistics as proof, that many people
suffer from a feeling of helplessness and unimportance in modern
technological society. He discusses the dehumanizing effects of
working in America. In white-collar jobs, Davis writes, the
bureaucratic framework forces workers to give up personal freedom,
originality, and spontaneity [Davis 1981, p. 118-120]. The
white-collar worker goes to work every morning, performs his appointed
tasks according to the company organizational structure, and leaves in
the evening. His schedule is usually rigidly organized, and he has no
time during the workday to relieve tensions and frustrations that
build up inside. The industrial worker is no better off. Companies
hire consultants to design the most efficient, most profitable, layout
of the company. Workers labor in robot-like fashion, performing a
series of tasks, over and over again, for the entire day [Davis 1981,
p. 122-125].

Robert Blauner has also written a great deal about the alienation of
the worker in modern industrial society. Along similar lines to Davis'
concept of dehumanization, Blauner argues that the modern worker feels
a sense of alienation from the workplace. Alienation, Blauner writes,
is comprised of many problems, two of which are a detachment of the
worker from any sort of meaningful control or relationship with his
work, and a sense of unimportance in the workplace [Blauner 1968, p.
1-15].

Powerlessness is sometimes an inevitable part of modern industrial
work. If there is a fast-paced system of production it may be so
inflexible that the worker must work along rigid guidelines. But this
can lead to problems. What happens when the worker is unable to
deviate from those rules set out? They are then, Blauner writes,
powerless and become frustrated [Blauner 1968, p. 16]. Another
important aspect related to alienation, or dehumanization, of the
workplace, according to Blauner, is the problem of meaninglessness.
The modern capitalist economy is constantly striving for optimum
efficiency of production. This, in some types of industry, tends to
force people into limited roles where the worker performs repetitive
tasks throughout the day. In order for the company to be streamlined
and efficient, it must compartmentalize the worker. The importance and
the meaning behind doing his job may become lost to such a worker. He
may lose track of his place in the production of the entire product,
and may therefore lose any drive to excel or feel any pride in his
work [Blauner 1968, p. 22-24]. Of course, it is important to realize
that Blauner was writing about an earlier industrial period. However,
I think that he had a very significant grasp of a fundamental problem
with modern society. How can the autonomy and individuality of the
worker be reconciled with the need for business to constantly
innovate, increase production, and stay competitive? In summary, if
the worker is put in a stressful job where he has no control, and
where the job at times seems pointless, it should not come as a
surprise when the worker feels a sense of malaise about his place in
society.

Some companies recognize the problems that result from this inflexible
and demeaning work environment. They try to humanize the workplace a
little bit more. Breaks from work, when the worker can relax, and
release tension accumulated while working, are granted; some companies
try to make the worker feel more appreciated. They give workers better
sounding job titles, allow them to have some input into the decision
making process. But Davis argues that what is done is not nearly
enough, and that the humanization of the workplace will take a long
time to complete. The co-dependents, as Kaminer points out, try to
adjust by going to therapy, support groups, or trying self-help
support.

But is there, perhaps, another group in society, one that refuses to
be put in the stressful conditions which the modern workplace imposes?
David Wagner argues that some of the homeless in society may be
deviants who refuse to submit their individuality to the workplace.
His book is a case study of a city in the north-eastern section of the
United States. Wagner does not reveal the true name of his city, but
refers to it as North City. In his interviews with the homeless of
North City, Wagner found homeless people who stated, in various ways,
that their self-respect and individualism were more important to them
than the minimal rewards the work system offered them. This population
preferred jobs where managers did not ``hassle them'' [Davis 1981, p.
86], and they refused jobs which they thought were boring, or jobs
which they thought were below their standards [Wagner 1993, p. 75-79].
In effect, these people refused to be dehumanized by the society's
work system, and believed that expressing their individuality this way
made them more human, regardless of what society thought about them.

It is important to realize that this was only one case study of a
single city, and does not necessarily reflect upon all homeless.
Nevertheless, I argue that the problems these homeless had with how
the modern work-force operates look very significant. Why is it that
so many of these homeless see the low-paying jobs as a very real
danger to their individualism?



Anti-technology Revolution?

Unabomer's conclusion, his discussion of the anti-technology
revolution, is weak. Unabomer simply argues that we must destroy
technology. Unabomer fails to lay out even the most basic of goals,
but simply urges us to rise up in revolt against modern technology.
Unabomer's explanation for this lack of plan is that nobody can lay
out a new society on paper. While this may be true, and may justify no
further discussion in his mind, it leaves us with a very large problem
with his thesis. I argue that nobody is going to take part in a
massive anti-technology movement without a viable plan or goal.

How, then, could he have solved this problem? Part of the solution
could be to draw upon the wealth of ideas from other anti-technology
movements. Schumacher, Norgaard, and Davis have all argued that social
reform to fix all our problems is possible, and each gives us some
ideas about how, and why, it might be accomplished.

Schumacher argues that many of our problems can be resolved by
changing how we view production. The burdens of production eased by
technology are those of mass production. Because of the ability for
this technology to generate an enormous number of goods at cheap
prices, the work available for skilled artisans has declined.
Schumacher writes that this is ``mass production,'' by the machine,
against the ``production of the masses,'' by artisans. The production
of the masses, Schumacher writes, shifts the technology toward being a
means to an end, instead of an end in and of itself. The goal for the
production of the masses is an improved society. The happiness and
well-being of the society would be placed before the profit of the
individual. Schumacher wants a move away from high-technology toward
what he calls intermediate technology. He points out that it is not an
attempt to revert to primitive tools, but an attempt to move toward
cheaper, simpler tools that still help us get our jobs done.
